This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last. In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market. But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere. For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding. Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right. The old challenges and the new ones have something in common. Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”. Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed. Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing. Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way. Why Europe acts in some crises but not others It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome. My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others. When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another. Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion. Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO. Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing. What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back. Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is certain and has to be paid straight away. Both the old challenges and the new ones are of this kind. Take capital markets. We have all agreed for more than a decade that Europe needs a capital markets union. But building it means taking on vested interests now, for gains that arrive years later. Each year without it, more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding. Yet no single year’s loss is large enough to overcome the resistance to change. We have seen this again in recent weeks. The Council has just agreed its position on strengthening the supervision of capital markets, which is welcome. But the position weakens the European supervisor’s ability to take effective decisions and includes too many carve-outs. Our dependencies raise the same problem. Reducing them means paying for new capacity now, against a threat that may never materialise. One recent estimate suggests that raising Europe’s share of the world’s AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030 would require investment of around €1.3 trillion. [ 1 ] But as long as we can buy computing power from foreign providers and frontier AI models remain available to us, the case for paying that price is hard to make. In both, the cost of inaction is real, whether it is a loss we are already suffering or a danger we may face tomorrow. But it rarely becomes visible enough to build the broad consensus for change that we found for the pandemic or for Ukraine. This is the central problem of European policymaking. We can see the problem early, but we can act only once it has become impossible to ignore. And by then, almost by definition, it is too late. Lost industries are very hard to win back, and once a dependency has been used against us, our sovereignty is already exposed. Think of the euro area debt crisis. The scale of Greece’s difficulties was clear long before Europe acted decisively to strengthen its institutions. We paid a much higher price than if we had acted earlier, including a six-quarter recession. We often hear that policymakers in Europe do not understand the problems they face. I think they do. The difficulty is that they are asked to impose visible costs on their citizens today, for benefits that will only become apparent over time, before a majority is convinced that action is needed. These are among the hardest decisions in public life, and I have a great deal of sympathy for those who have to take them. At the ECB, we have had to take some of them too. Acting early at the ECB Economic sovereignty is not an objective in itself for us. Our primary objective is price stability, and the Treaty also gives us the tasks of issuing money and promoting the smooth operation of payment systems. But a changing world bears directly on those tasks, and during my term it has confronted us with slow-moving risks of our own. We have faced decisions of this kind in three areas. In each, we had to choose whether to invest early in something whose value would only become clear later. The first area was retail payments. Since the euro was introduced, Europeans have had a single means of payment that works everywhere in the euro area: euro cash. But for card payments, we have relied on providers from outside Europe. International card schemes handle more than 60% of our card payments, and 14 of the 21 euro area countries have no domestic scheme at all. [ 2 ] For a long time, this did not seem to matter, because cash was still the dominant means of payment. The international schemes worked well, and no one had ever cut Europe off. The private sector tried more than once to build a European alternative, but each attempt ran into the same vicious circle: merchants will not adopt a scheme that few customers use, and customers will not use one that few merchants accept. But cash is playing a smaller role as more of our spending moves online, where more than a third of our day-to-day spending now takes place. [ 3 ] And the geopolitical climate has changed. We have already seen judges of the International Criminal Court living in Europe, some of them European citizens, lose the use of their bank cards overnight. So we concluded that Europe needed a digital equivalent of cash: the digital euro. It will give Europeans a means of payment that runs on European infrastructure. And as legal tender, it will have to be accepted throughout the euro area wherever digital payments are possible, which will break the vicious circle in a way that private initiatives could not. Private payment providers will then have open rails on which to compete. Because a project of this scale takes years to build, we had to start well before the need became pressing. If the legislation is adopted by the end of this year, we aim to be ready for a first issuance in 2029. The second area was wholesale markets. With blockchain technology, securities can now be tokenised, so that they are issued, traded and settled on a single platform. With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity. But the window for seizing it is limited. The market for tokenised assets is still small, worth around €23 billion worldwide in March, but it was five times its size a year earlier. [ 4 ] As it grows, its standards and practices will take shape. If they develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. And as our capital markets have taught us, once standards and practices have diverged, they are very hard to bring back together. That is why, in September, we launched Pontes, which allows tokenised transactions to settle in central bank money on Eurosystem infrastructure, under European rules. Every platform now has access to a common settlement asset, so liquidity no longer has to be divided between them. Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism settled a €1 billion digitally native bond on Pontes. Through Appia, we are working with market participants towards an integrated European market, including common standards. But infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators. The third area was the international role of the euro. For most of its history, the ECB took a neutral view of the euro’s international role. Shortly before my term began, it moved to a more supportive line, and during my term we have acted on it. A stronger international role for the euro matters for our monetary policy, and it can support Europe’s growth and sovereignty in the world we now face. Europe faces large investment needs, from defence to the technologies on which our autonomy depends, and a currency that investors around the world want to hold lowers the cost of financing them. In a world of more frequent shocks, the more of our trade is invoiced in euro, the less exposed we are to swings in exchange rates. So, where it supports our own mandate, we have made the euro easier to use abroad. We are linking TIPS, our instant payment system, with fast payment systems in other regions. We have also strengthened our international liquidity lines as a backstop. In February we made EUREP, our repo facility for central banks, permanent and open to central banks worldwide. More than 30 central banks have already expressed interest. And we are working to keep our swap lines fit for purpose in a more fragmented world. They will be more accessible, too. The primary objective of these lines is to protect the transmission of our monetary policy in a crisis, by limiting spillovers from abroad into our own markets. But they also support the euro’s global role. A reserve manager who knows that euro securities can be turned into euro liquidity without a fire sale has more reason to hold them in normal times. What lessons can we draw? In our own field, we have tried to act on slow-moving risks early, before they were fully visible. I would draw three lessons from this experience. The first is that it is far easier to take the long view with a European mandate. I should be frank about our own case. If we were able to commit early, it was largely because of how we are built. Our mandate is defined for the euro area as a whole. Our horizon is long, and the Governing Council can decide by majority. That made our decisions easier than those facing national governments, which have to weigh concentrated opposition at home against benefits that are spread across Europe, while reaching agreement with partners who face the same constraints. But this is no reason for fatalism. It tells us something important about how Europe needs to be built. Where we agree that a challenge requires a European solution, we should strengthen the European institutions that can provide it, so that this trade-off weighs less heavily. In capital markets, that means a European supervisor able to take effective decisions. In technology, where projects such as chip plants and data centres need European scale, it means public-private partnerships at European level, with public money, including from the EU budget, taking the first losses and drawing in private capital. The second lesson is that we should design our response, wherever we can, so that it pays off even if the worst never happens. That makes it easier to build support for acting early, because we no longer need to agree on how likely the danger is. The digital euro is an example. Even if Europe is never cut off from the international card schemes, it will still be better placed, because we have designed the digital euro on open standards that allow any provider to offer services across the whole euro area. The same principle can guide other choices that require large commitments. Take defence. EU countries spent around €420 billion on defence last year, a fifth more than the year before, and are set to spend over €450 billion this year, [ 5 ] at a time when budgets are stretched and many other priorities compete for the same resources. But if more of that money is spent on research and development, it can benefit the whole economy, whatever the security outlook. Today, we spend ten times less on defence R&D than the United States, relative to the size of our economy. [ 6 ] Recent ECB analysis suggests that, over the long term, each additional euro of public R&D spending can generate almost 2.5 euros of GDP. [ 7 ] Not every choice can be designed this way. Some protection is simply insurance, and we should be honest that it has a price. But the more of our response we can design to pay off in every future, the easier it becomes to act in time. The third lesson is more personal. I have faced these decisions throughout my career as a policymaker, at national, European and international level. However carefully we design our choices, some uncertainty always remains, and someone has to take responsibility for deciding. The hardest judgement is to recognise when waiting has become the riskier choice, before the evidence is beyond doubt. At that point, leaders have to find the courage to make the case for acting, before a majority is ready to hear it. And those who act early must be prepared to go without thanks. As Henry Kissinger observed, “it is in the nature of successful policies that posterity forgets how easily things might have been otherwise.” So we should do everything we can to make acting early easier, by doing more at European level and by designing policies that pay off whatever the future holds. But we will also need leaders who believe in Europe and are prepared to fight for it. Conclusion Let me conclude. Over these seven years, I have seen Europe do things that were once thought impossible, when events had made the way ahead clear. The question now is whether it can act with the same resolve before the need becomes impossible to ignore. At the ECB, we have tried to do that in our own field. Whether we judged well, others will decide in time. But I hope I leave an institution that has helped give Europe more integration and more sovereignty than it had when I arrived. Much of what remains lies with others, and with those who will lead Europe in the years ahead. I am confident that they will find the conviction to act in time. Thank you. Schnitzer, M. et al. body:
How to transfer your chat history into Gemini ICYMI: Transfer your history from other AI apps into Gemini. Nov 19, 2026 Switch to Gemini without starting from scratch. Here’s how to bring your context, preferences, and chat history from a different AI assistant into Gemini. Open your Gemini import settings and copy our prompt. Paste it into your previous AI tool to generate a summary of your preferences. Paste the response into Gemini. Export a ZIP file of your chat history from your previous provider's account settings. Upload the ZIP archive in Gemini settings to pick up conversations right where you left off. title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
body: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs NVIDIA and Microsoft expand tools for enterprises to customize AI models and deploy applications across cloud and local infrastructure. November 19, 2026 by Dave Salvator 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work. An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model , developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation. Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services. Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA. Visit NVIDIA at Ignite for demonstrations spanning enterprise applications, robotics, accelerated data processing and local computing, with hardware including an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack and RTX Spark devices. View NVIDIA sessions, hands-on labs and booth theater presentations . title: How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale.
body: How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale. Nov 19, 2026 Today, in new research published on the cover of Science , Google Quantum AI demonstrated that contextuality — a quantum property scientists believe powers certain quantum algorithms — survives at scale on our quantum processor. What gives quantum computers their unique power? While entanglement usually gets the spotlight, theory suggests that a deeper quantum property called contextuality may power certain quantum algorithms. In simple terms, contextuality means a system’s properties aren’t fixed in advance; what you measure depends on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it. Until recently, this effect had mostly been shown in small systems of just a few particles. Our paper in Science now demonstrates this at scale on our quantum processor. Using it, our qubits won a well-known coordination game 98.3% of the time, beating the 88.9% classical limit, and outperformed constrained classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits. These tests also serve as a sensitive new method to catch subtle hardware errors, helping pave the way for real-world applications like chemistry and materials science.

title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
body: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents See how developers are combining AI agents with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build simulation applications, test physical behavior and guide improvements. November 19, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Nyhamna_footage_take5_30s.mp4 AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions. Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation. AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view. Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream f or a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task. NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls. Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task. Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior. Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released. NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries : ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton , which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries. The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. Explore his open source demo f or build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills. Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/microducks-icu-16x9-1920x1080-new.mp4 Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting. AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours. Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗 Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

title: A smarter way to track and buy clean energy
body: A smarter way to track and buy clean energy Nov 19, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Granular certificates are a next-generation tool to ensure more accurate, impactful clean energy buying. Jenna Stauffer Head of Strategic Priorities, Climate Operations Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We are advancing Granular Certificates to track clean energy by hour and location, providing clear pricing signals that encourage smarter grid management. These tools help you match electricity use with local clean energy production, supporting a more stable power system. You can watch our new video to learn how these certificates help developers, energy asset owners, and the grid. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We use Granular Certificates to track clean energy supply by specific hour and geographic location. Trading volume in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic region increased 437% during our recent monthly spot auctions. Our support for the Registry Acceleration Fund helps organizations verify and track hourly energy data. These certificates provide new revenue streams for battery storage operators and improve grid stability overall. We reduced our Scope 2 emissions by 3% while managing a 37% increase in electricity load. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are using new tools called Granular Certificates to track clean energy by the hour and location. These certificates help us match our electricity use with local solar or wind power, even when the sun is not shining. By creating clear price signals, this system encourages companies to build more batteries and clean energy projects where they are needed most. This helps us manage our power use and supports a cleaner, more stable energy grid. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Granular Certificates (GCs) are next-generation clean energy instruments. They precisely track supply by hour and location, helping companies match their electricity load with local clean energy. Their hourly pricing signals encourage the development of clean generation and energy storage when and where it is needed most. These instruments can incentivize improved grid management, and they can help accelerate the deployment of advanced clean technologies, leading to a cleaner, more stable power system. But like any nascent solution, the foundational building blocks need to be in place first. We first started piloting GCs in 2021 and, in just five years, they’ve transitioned from early concept to real-world certificates, traded on specific hours. We’re continuing to take actions to accelerate both our own procurement and the global GC ecosystem. Here are three key ways the GC ecosystem advanced this year: 1. The GC marketplace is growing. Marketplaces are critical because they establish transparent hourly pricing signals and help simplify processes for those new to hourly procurement. LevelTen, in partnership with the Granular Certificate Trading Alliance (GCTA) and the Intercontinental Exchange, launched the Granular Certificate Marketplace in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic grid region PJM in October 2025. Since that first auction, trading volume has increased 437% in just one year , with Google participating in every monthly spot auction. This increased trading volume generates clear pricing signals, with higher premiums occurring during evening hours. By demonstrating when buyers need clean energy most, GCs can incentivize suppliers to operate or build clean energy to meet this demand. 2. Global registries help with tracking and verification. Almost every corporate clean energy buyer uses registries, which track and verify their clean energy purchases via instruments like monthly or annual energy attribute certificates (EACs). Registries help also ensure EACs are not double counted, supporting unique clean energy claims. However, until recently, the vast majority of registries didn’t have the technical capabilities to accommodate GCs. To help address those gaps, Google supported the GCTA in establishing the Registry Acceleration Fund . The fund awarded grants to five of the largest organizations that operate registries, which collectively issue or track 4,000 TWh of certificates in over 70+ countries. As of today, one of these organizations has met their technical milestones that would allow them to transfer, verify, and retire GCs. The remaining four organizations are expected to finish in early 2027. This will add critical functionality needed for these instruments to scale, including standardization of the hourly data and traceability to one clear owner. 3. GCs are driving real value. Despite the GC market’s nascency, its potential benefits are moving from academic research concepts towards demonstrating real impact. For example, in a recent GCTA white paper , clean energy developers and asset operators shared real-life perspectives on granular matching. These developers explained that pricing signals from GCs can help them maximize existing energy assets in the near-term, while helping them make crucial decisions about project siting and technology diversification in the longer term. In addition, Google, esVolta, Quintrace, and LevelTen helped prove a new revenue stream for battery energy storage system operators. We partnered to pilot the first GCs for storage systems, shifting solar generation to match our targeted demand hours. This could not have happened without hourly tracking and verification via GCs. Hear more firsthand accounts of the benefits of GCs to developers, energy asset owners, and the grid in our new video . In addition to the maturing global ecosystem, we’ve also continued to evolve our use of GCs to help manage Google’s emissions. We’ll always prioritize applying new, long-term clean energy agreements, and the underlying hourly GCs, first. Even with a large clean energy portfolio, the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow exactly when we need it to. Marketplace GCs help fill those gaps. At the same time, our purchases help build a stronger market where GCs can be bought and sold quickly, easily, and in large quantities — creating clearer price signals and providing granular options for growing numbers of buyers. We used a smaller amount of marketplace GCs alongside a much larger amount of clean energy agreements to help lower our Scope 2 market-based emissions by 3% from 2024 to 2025 , despite a 37% electricity load increase. We will include a limited amount of marketplace GCs in our 24/7 CFE performance in the future. Looking ahead, these tools will become even more important to develop. The recently released net zero standard of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) will require reporting on hourly matching performance for large energy users, and the GHG Protocol (GHGP) is evaluating the introduction of hourly emissions reporting. We will continue to work on developing and advancing GCs — not just for our own efforts, but to ensure others can use these tools to build a better energy system. In the latest episode of Ads Decoded, Ads Product Liaison Ginny Marvin sits down with product leads Sagar Shah and Al Nevarez to explore how A/B testing validates AI Max features, budget shifts, and Smart Bidding strategies. Three key rules to guide your testing: Start with templated setups: Pre-built templates isolate single variables, split traffic 50/50, and minimize setup errors for cleaner data. Focus on business outcomes: Measure qualified conversions rather than shallow proxies, and give tests four to six weeks to account for conversion lag. Match confidence to decision scope: An 80% confidence interval works well for directional tweaks. Reserve 95% certainty for major structural overhauls. body: See some of the work from Google Flow and Flow Music Sessions artists Nov 19, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link See how creators across every discipline are bringing their visions to life with Google Flow and Google Flow Music. Brianna Doyle Head of Community, Google Labs Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We are sharing new visual projects and audio tools created by artists and musicians during our recent Google Flow sessions. These projects demonstrate how our latest models and features can support your creative workflows, from developing animated shorts to building custom music plugins. You can view the artists' work and try remixing their audio tools on our website to see how these resources fit into your own projects. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Brianna Doyle, Head of Community at Google Labs, shares visual projects created during our Flow Sessions. Artists used our AI creative studio to develop television pitches, animated shorts, and personal narrative projects. Musicians and producers built custom audio tools, plugins, and instruments using Spaces in Google Flow Music. You can explore these creative projects and remix the audio tools to support your own work. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are working with artists and musicians to test our Google Flow creative tools. These creators used our software to build animated shorts, visual projects, and custom music plugins like vocal processors or digital instruments. You can view their finished projects and try remixing their audio tools to see how these features fit your own creative process. We hope these examples inspire you to experiment with new ways to make art and music. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Through Flow Sessions and Flow Music Sessions, we’re partnering directly with creatives to hear what matters most to them. This dialogue helps us build products that are useful, tailored to their work, and that helps enable creatives to build what they’ve been dreaming to build. During our last six-week Flow Sessions, artists explored our AI creative studio, Google Flow . They developed visual projects, ranging from a pitch for a television series, animated shorts, and personal narratives, while experimenting with new workflows to see how our latest models can support their unique styles. Today we’re sharing a look at the visual projects from this group of artists: “A Lucky Greyhound” by Matias Collado “Brood” by Siri Lee “Roger & The Chicken” by River Davis “UNFIXED” by Jeehyun Kim “MIA” by Daniel Castro “Reality Drop” by Johana Kroft “How to Crack an Egg” by Luke Roberts “Starling” by Ian Bradley “The Catch” by Nate Talbot In addition to the visual projects, for Flow Music Sessions, we brought together musicians and producers to take a similar approach to experimenting with new workflows and tools. They focused on Spaces , a feature within Google Flow Music , to create bespoke audio tools, plugins, mini music apps, new instruments, and digital artifacts that can be used directly in any creative workflow. Check out the Spaces they created to get inspired, and you can try remixing their work to see how this approach can work for you: Bloom Cycles : A vocal plugin that uses your webcam to shift your voice in real time based on your hand gestures. Track Arranger : A songwriting tool that helps turn short loops into a full song structure with verses, choruses, and drops. Mel’s Dreamscape Vocals : A bright, pop-focused vocal processor packed with pro presets and easy tuning tools. Marble and Metal Visualisers : A 3D interactive visualizer that creates custom graphics reacting dynamically to live audio or uploaded music. Tune Sampler : A vintage-style console plugin inspired by 90s hip-hop gear designed to shape audio with analog warmth. Mirage Sampler : A playful software instrument that lets you easily drag and drop audio samples to flip them into unique textures and instruments. We’re grateful for the opportunity to partner closely with such talented creatives, and learn how our tools can best support them. If you’re interested in participating in Flow Sessions, you can learn more here , and follow for updates on Flow Music Sessions.
