title: Cumberland Medical Center Agrees to Improve Accessible Parking and Pay $25,000 to Resolve ADA Allegations
body: Press Release Cumberland Medical Center Agrees to Improve Accessible Parking and Pay $25,000 to Resolve ADA Allegations Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Tennessee Public Affairs NASHVILLE – Cumberland Medical Center, Inc., a hospital in Crossville, Tennessee, has agreed to improve accessibility in its parking lots and pay $25,000 to resolve allegations that its parking facilities did not comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), announced U.S. Attorney Braden H. Boucek for the Middle District of Tennessee. Under the settlement, the hospital will pay a $20,000 civil penalty and $5,000 to compensate the complainant. It also will make changes to provide the required number of accessible car and van parking spaces and access aisles, with accessible spaces located along the shortest accessible routes to the facility entrances they serve. Cumberland Medical Center cooperated with the United States throughout the investigation, and Cumberland Medical Center desired to improve its ADA compliance without litigation. The matter began with a complaint from a man with a mobility disability who reported that, while visiting his hospitalized wife several times a day in September 2023, he encountered accessible parking spaces farther from the hospital’s main entrance than other parking spaces. He alleged that the arrangement required him to walk farther than necessary. Following a 2025 site survey, the United States identified alleged accessibility deficiencies in parking areas serving the hospital’s main entrance, Maternity Center, Day Surgery, Hyperbaric and Wound Clinic, Admitting/Outpatient Clinic, Diagnostic Center, Cancer Center, and Cumberland Medical Plaza. The ADA requires public accommodation, including hospitals, to remove barriers to access when readily achievable and to ensure that covered alterations are accessible to the maximum extent feasible. Cumberland Medical Center cooperated with the United States during the investigation and agreed to resolve the matter without litigation. The settlement remains in effect for three years, during which the U.S. Attorney’s Office will monitor compliance. Assistant U.S. Attorney Ellen Bowden McIntyre investigated the complaint and negotiated the settlement, with assistance from Paralegal Elisabete Lopes. The civil claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only, and there has been no determination of liability. For information about the ADA, visit ada.gov, call the Justice Department’s ADA Information Line at 800-514-0301 (voice) or 800-514-0383 (TTY), or email ada.complaint@usdoj.gov. #### Contact Steve Stanley Public Affairs Officer Steve.Stanley2@usdoj.gov (615) 401-6615 Updated November 19, 2026 Component USAO - Tennessee, Middle

title: Two Mexican nationals indicted for methamphetamine trafficking
body: Press Release Two Mexican nationals indicted for methamphetamine trafficking Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of California SACRAMENTO, Calif. — A federal grand jury returned a two-count indictment today against Yair Contreras Gomez, 22, a Mexican national residing in Portland, Oregon, and Pablo Lopez Morales, 29, a Mexican national residing in Sacramento, California, charging them with conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine and charging Contreras Gomez with possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced. According to court documents, on multiple occasions between July 29, 2026, and Aug. 31, 2026, Contreras Gomez directed Lopez Morales to bring loads of methamphetamine from southern California to Portland. On Aug. 31, law enforcement officers intercepted one of these loads during a traffic stop while Lopez Morales was traveling northbound on Interstate 5 through Shasta County. The officers seized approximately 30 pounds of methamphetamine from inside the door panels of the vehicle. The Drug Enforcement Administration conducted the investigation with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations and the California Highway Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorney David W. Spencer is prosecuting the case. If convicted, the defendants face a mandatory minimum of 10 years in prison, a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison, and a $10 million fine. Any sentence, however, would be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables. The charges are only allegations; the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Sacramento is composed of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, Northern California High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area, Central Valley High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area, and the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California. title: Pennsylvania Man Sentenced to Nearly Four Years in Prison for Detonating an Explosive Device at Night Under Former Supervisor’s Vehicle
body: Press Release Pennsylvania Man Sentenced to Nearly Four Years in Prison for Detonating an Explosive Device at Night Under Former Supervisor’s Vehicle Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Jersey A Pennsylvania man was sentenced today to 46 months in prison for denotating an explosive device under a vehicle that was parked at his former supervisor’s residence, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced. Michael Patrick Takacs, Jr., 44, of Warminster, Pennsylvania, previously pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Karen M. Williams in Camden federal court to one count of transporting an explosive with the knowledge and intent that it would be used to intimidate an individual and that it would be used unlawfully to damage and destroy property. According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court: Just before three o’clock in the morning on July 26, 2025, Takacs detonated an improvised explosive device, commonly referred to as an “IED,” under his former supervisor’s vehicle in a residential neighborhood in Delran, New Jersey.  Takacs detonated the IED in retaliation for being fired from his place of employment a few months earlier.  Despite taking steps to evade law enforcement detection by removing his license plate from his vehicle when transporting the IED from Pennsylvania to New Jersey and leaving his cell phone at home, law enforcement identified Takacs as the perpetrator and charged him less than two weeks after the explosion. In addition to the prison term, Judge Williams ordered Takacs to pay restitution to the victim and to serve three years of supervised release. U.S. Attorney Frazer credited the following with the investigation leading to the charges against Takacs: special agents and joint terrorism task force officers of the FBI, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy in Newark and Special Agent in Charge Wayne A. Jacobs in Philadelphia; the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, under the direction of U.S. Attorney David Metcalf; the New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness, under the direction of Director Thomas G. Hauck; the New Jersey State Police, under the direction of Superintendent Jeanne Hengemuhle; the Burlington County Prosecutor’s Office, under the direction of LaChia L. Bradshaw; the Delran (NJ) Township Police Department, under the direction of Acting Chief Matthew J. Gasper; the Warminster (PA) Township Police Department under the direction of Chief James Donnelly III; the Bucks County (PA) Sheriff’s Office, under the direction of Sheriff Daniel Ceisler; and the Bucks County District Attorney’s Office, under the direction of District Attorney Joe Khan. The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Casey S. Smith and Vincent D. Romano of the National Security Unit in Newark, with assistance from the U.S. Department of Justice’s Counterterrorism Section of the National Security Division. ### Defense counsel: Thomas Young, Esq. Updated November 19, 2026 Component USAO - New Jersey Press Release Number: 26-256

title: Warren County Man Sentenced to 30 Years for Child Exploitation Offenses
body: Press Release Warren County Man Sentenced to 30 Years for Child Exploitation Offenses Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Jersey TRENTON, N.J. – A Warren County, New Jersey, man was sentenced in connection with his sexual exploitation of minors, United States Attorney Robert Frazer announced today. Dennis Stout, 44, of Phillipsburg, New Jersey, was sentenced today to 360 months’ imprisonment followed by a life term of supervised release before U.S. District Court Judge Zahid N. Quraishi in Trenton federal court on charges of production and distribution of child pornography. According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court: From January through December 2024, Stout distributed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) across multiple social media platforms, including CSAM that he produced depicting his sexual abuse of a minor. Law enforcement discovered Stout’s activities on December 13, 2024, when an undercover officer engaged with Stout’s online persona. Authorities identified Stout as the individual operating the account and arrested him the following day. U.S. Attorney Frazer credited special agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Newark Field Office, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Stefanie Roddy, with the investigation.  U.S. Attorney Frazer also thanked the FBI’s Washington Field Office and the Hunterdon County and Warren County Prosecutor’s Offices for their assistance in the investigation. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) in the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit: https://www.justice.gov/psc . U.S. Attorney Frazer has announced proactive steps to connect with New Jersey’s families and communities, bringing training opportunities and resources through direct outreach. Organizations and community members interested in arranging prevention programming or learning more about available resources can contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey at USANJ.CommunityOutreach@usdoj.gov . The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Matt Belgiovine, Co-Chief of the General Crimes Unit. ### Defense counsel: Laura Sayler, Esq., Office of the Federal Public Defender Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - New Jersey Press Release Number: 26-257

title: Registered Sex Offender Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Possession of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Registered Sex Offender Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Possession of Child Pornography Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts Defendant was on state probation for possession of child pornography at the time of offense BOSTON – A registered sex offender from Holyoke has been sentenced in federal court in Springfield, Mass. for possessing child pornography. Justin Ouimette, 35, was sentenced on Nov. 17, 2026 by U.S. District Court Judge Mark Mastroianni to 10 years in prison, to be followed by 15 years of supervised release. In August 2026 , Ouimette pleaded guilty to possession of child pornography. Ouimette was charged by complaint in May 2025 and has remained in custody since that time. Ouimette was identified as the owner of a Dropbox account uploading child sexual abuse material (CSAM). During the search of Ouimette’s residence, an electronic device was found to contain hundreds of files of CSAM depicting children as young as toddlers. Subsequent searches of Ouimette’s cloud storage accounts revealed hundreds of additional files depicting CSAM. Ouimette was previously convicted in Massachusetts Superior Court of possession of child pornography in October 2022 and was on state probation when he committed this new offense. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Caroline Merck of the Springfield Office prosecuted the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: Buffalo woman arrested, charged with possession of large quantities of fentanyl and cocaine following Homeland Security Task Force investigation
body: Press Release Buffalo woman arrested, charged with possession of large quantities of fentanyl and cocaine following Homeland Security Task Force investigation Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of New York BUFFALO, N.Y. - U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Keionna Goins, 48, of Buffalo, NY, was arrested and charged by criminal complaint with possession with intent to distribute a large quantity of fentanyl and cocaine, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, and a $1,000,000 fine. According to the criminal complaint, on November 17, 2026, the Homeland Security Task Force and Buffalo Police executed a search warrant at a Comstock Avenue residence. Goins, the lone occupant in the residence, was encountered at the front door of the residence, handcuffed and taken into custody. During the search of the residence, investigators seized approximately 10,166 grams of suspected fentanyl, and 2,697 grams of suspected cocaine. They also recovered a large quantity of suspected methamphetamine, approximately 633 grams of suspected MDMA, a large amount of cash, and a loaded .38 caliber revolver. “This case goes to the heart of the mission of the Homeland Security Task Force,” stated U.S. Attorney DiGiacomo. “Law enforcement at all levels working together to remove literally hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of dangerous narcotics from the streets of Buffalo, the type of narcotics trafficking that often results in violence in our community. The Buffalo Homeland Security Task Force is tops in removing drugs and bringing to justice the criminals that peddle them.” HSI Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Patrone stated, “Every day, we see the scourges of fentanyl leave a lasting, costly impact on our neighborhoods — it poisons our communities, fuels violence and endangers the vulnerable. The progress announced today puts those who profit from harm on notice: if you exploit our communities to move dangerous contraband that victimizes members of our communities, you will face a coordinated law enforcement response. HSI Buffalo and our HSTF partners will continue to work across agencies to disrupt criminal networks, protect the public, and strengthen the security of the communities we serve.” Goins made an initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Jeremiah J. McCarthy and was held pending a detention hearing on November 20, 2026. This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Buffalo comprises agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigations, Department of Homeland Security Enforcement and Removal Operations, Customs and Border Protection, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the U.S. Coast Guard Investigative Service, the U.S. Marshals Service, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the U.S. Secret Service, and the Diplomatic Security Service, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of New York. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney MacCaelin Sedita. The complaint is the result of an investigation by Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Patrone, the Buffalo Police Department, under the direction of Chief Erika Shields, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, firearms, and Explosives, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Bryan DiGirolamo, New York Field Division. The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. # # # # Contact Barbara Burns 716-843-5817 Updated November 19, 2026 Topics Homeland Security Task Force Drug Trafficking Opioids Component USAO - New York, Western

title: Highs Member Sentenced to 460 Months in Prison for RICO Conspiracy and Role in Murder of Innocent Bystander in North Minneapolis
body: Press Release Highs Member Sentenced to 460 Months in Prison for RICO Conspiracy and Role in Murder of Innocent Bystander in North Minneapolis Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Minnesota MINNEAPOLIS – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that William Johnson, aka “Lil Will,” 36, was sentenced to 460 months in prison before U.S. District Judge Nancy E. Brasel on November 19, 2026. Johnson is one of 40 Highs gang members charged in the case U.S. v. Montez Brown et al. (23-cr-160). On January 21, 2026, a federal jury found Johnson guilty on one count of first-degree murder and one count of Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) conspiracy. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, the Highs gang began to claim areas of north Minneapolis in 2004, and since then, its members have ruthlessly protected their territory including against their rival gang, the Lows. The victims of the violence went beyond the members and associates of the gangs, but also innocent adults and children who simply live within the gangs’ territories. Image 1: Overview of Highs and Lows territories which are separated by West Broadway Avenue in Minneapolis Between 2018 and 2023, in north Minneapolis alone and where the Highs and Lows claim their territory, there were over 150 homicides, 1,150 gunshot victims, and 2,000 recovered firearms. Residents living in the two gangs’ territories live in fear of being robbed, shot with a machine gun, or losing a loved one to fentanyl trafficked by the Highs and Lows. Johnson’s ties to the Highs began at least before October 2016, and he has social media posts dating back to when he was 13 years old announcing his affiliation with a clique associated with the Highs gang. Officers found Johnson on at least two occasions riding in a vehicle with other Highs members. During one of those occasions, a car stop in March 2017, officers recovered a 9mm Glock with Johnson’s fingerprints on it that was hidden in the passenger door panel where Johnson was sitting. Johnson later pleaded guilty to unlawfully possessing the recovered firearm. On August 7, 2021, a prominent Highs member was shot and killed at a gas station that Highs members called, “the Murder Station.” The next day, Highs members gathered at a memorial at the gas station, including Johnson and others. Two Highs members then drove to Wally’s Food, a known Lows hangout spot and shot a Lows member in the back for retribution. Approximately two hours later, six Highs members rode in two cars to drive to another Lows hangout spot, the Skyline Market. One of the cars was driven by Johnson, with two Highs members as passengers. The second car, which was stolen, drove behind Johnson. The second car had the three remaining members, including one juvenile Highs member. Surveillance video shows that a male victim entered the Skyline Market just minutes before Johnson and two other Highs members arrived in the first car. Johnson’s two Highs associates then went into the store, both armed with guns. Johnson remained outside as the second car arrived. Inside the store, the two Highs members began shooting multiple rounds at the victim. The victim ran out of the store and across the street where the second car was driving past. The two Highs members continued to fire at the victim outside the store. Johnson watched as the two Highs associates came out of the store and repeatedly shot in the victim’s direction. The two Highs associates that were in the store then got back into the car that Johnson was driving, and Johnson sped away. The victim collapsed in a nearby alley, and two Highs members in the second car then fired more rounds at him. Law enforcement arrived within a minute, but the victim was pronounced dead at the hospital. The victim was not a member of any street gang. During the sentencing, Judge Brasel asked, “How many more opportunities does one person get?” She continued, “The answer today is no more.” “This long-term investigation revealed many sad examples like this where a murder was committed in retaliation for a prior shooting between rival gangs in Minneapolis,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Members of the Highs gang, including William Johnson, hunted down suspected rivals of the Lows gang on the streets of Minneapolis and gunned down a victim who turned out to not be a gang member. For years, this gang warfare in Minnesota caused death and destruction, and for innocent people to live in fear of getting killed. Charging and prosecuting cases against enterprises and criminal organizations bring positive change in these neighborhoods and stem violence so that innocent people can live their lives without fear. The Criminal Division has ensured and will continue to ensure that Minnesota streets are safer, and we will not stop until all of these shooters are locked up.” “The defendant was not a bystander or just a follower. He was the getaway driver for shooters whom he knew would murder someone in retribution. My office has continued to take down and dismantle this criminal enterprise. Residents of north Minneapolis have a right to live without fear of violence,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen. “Long-term investigations like this require extraordinary commitment from the people who work them,” said Special Agent in Charge Joseph Persails, of the ATF St. Paul Field Division. “The investigators and prosecutors who saw this case through never lost sight of the fact that an innocent man was killed and a community was routinely terrorized. Today's sentence delivers accountability for that violence and sends a message that those who bring fear and violence to our communities will be pursued until justice is served.” “The Highs, including this defendant, believed that much of north Minneapolis was their territory for decades. With this sentence, William Johnson found that those neighborhoods belong to the citizens of Minnesota,” said FBI Minneapolis Field Office Acting Special Agent in Charge Benni Jonsson. “Today’s sentence reflects this defendant’s role in the criminal enterprise-driven, cold-blood murder of an innocent community member. We hope the justice delivered from this outcome helps the victim’s family heal and shows the community that the FBI and our partners will ensure that justice finds those who seek to terrorize our neighborhoods for the benefit of a criminal organization.” “The violence, drug trafficking, and bloodshed associated with the Highs and Lows gangs in Minnesota is a threat to all community members in the region,” DEA Omaha Field Division Acting Special Agent in Charge Rafael Mattei said. “No one should live in fear of losing their life while out running errands. Let this serve as a reminder that law enforcement agencies at the state, local and federal level are working together, pooling resources and sharing intelligence. We’re building cases that have the potential to place these threatening offenders in prison for lengthy terms, as proven with today’s sentencing.” “Gang allegiance is a poor trade for freedom. William Johnson chose to take part in a criminal enterprise, and today’s sentence delivers the consequence of that choice,” said HSI St. Paul Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard. Those who advance organized crime should expect to be identified, charged, and held accountable. Our law enforcement partners will continue to dismantle criminal networks that endanger Minnesota communities.” “William Johnson and his fellow gang members treated human life as if it were disposable,” said Robert J. Kuszynski, Acting Special Agent in Charge, IRS Criminal Investigation, Chicago Field Office. “Darryl Wells should still be alive today. No prison sentence can undo the pain his family has endured, but this sentence should make clear that those who choose violence and murder must answer for the lives they destroy.” These cases against the Highs are a result of an investigation conducted by the ATF, FBI, Minneapolis Police Department, IRS Criminal Investigation, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office, Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, Minnesota Department of Corrections, with assistance from the U.S. Marshals Service, DEA, Homeland Security Investigations, and the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office. The Ramsey County Sheriff’s Office, Dakota County Sheriff’s Office, St. Paul Police Department, and numerous other law enforcement agencies contributed to this investigation through reports or evidence control. Assistant United States Attorney Albania Concepcion and Trial Attorneys Brian Lynch and Alyssa Levey-Weinstein of the Justice Department’s Violent Crime & Racketeering Section, prosecuted these cases. Note: This press release was updated on November 19, 2026, to include additional statements from the DEA and the U.S. District Judge. Contact usamn.pressoffice@usdoj.gov Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Components Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Minnesota

title: Columbia Man Pleads Guilty to Being a Felon in Possession of a Firearm
body: Press Release Columbia Man Pleads Guilty to Being a Felon in Possession of a Firearm Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Carolina COLUMBIA, S.C. — Kyreem Dreveon Tindal, 24, of Columbia, has pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm. On Aug. 1, 2023, Columbia Police Department conducted a lawful traffic stop of a vehicle in downtown Columbia after learning that the driver, who was driving under suspension, was live streaming from the vehicle with a passenger who had a firearm sitting in his lap. The passenger, Tindal, ran from the vehicle. Officers found Tindal hiding in nearby bushes and recovered the firearm Tindal dropped while running. The firearm had previously been reported stolen in Charlotte, N.C. DNA analysis of the firearm linked it to Tindal. Tindal has prior state convictions for assault and battery 1st degree and discharging a firearm into a dwelling. Tindal participated in the Ceasefire program hosted by the City of Columbia Police Department. The Ceasefire program identifies offenders who are at risk of future firearms offenses and introduces them to community resources such as substance abuse treatment and employment services. During participation in the program, law enforcement emphasizes the likelihood of future state and federal prosecution if participants, like Tindal, reoffend. Following his participation, Tindal was charged with an unrelated state offense, leading to the federal prosecution of the 2023 gun offense. Tindal faces a maximum penalty of 15 years in federal prison. He also faces a fine of up to $250,000, restitution, and three of supervision to follow the term of imprisonment.  United States District Judge Mary Geiger Lewis accepted the guilty plea and will sentence Tindal after receiving and reviewing a sentencing report prepared by the U.S. Probation Office. Tindal remains in custody awaiting sentencing. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms, Tobacco and Explosives and the Columbia Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Stacey D. Haynes is prosecuting the case. ### Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Neighborhoods Components Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) USAO - South Carolina

title: Ecuadorian National Pleads Guilty to Committing Several Truck Thefts, Including Stealing $100 Million in Jewelry from Brinks Truck
body: Press Release Ecuadorian National Pleads Guilty to Committing Several Truck Thefts, Including Stealing $100 Million in Jewelry from Brinks Truck Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California RIVERSIDE, California – An Ecuadorian national pleaded guilty today to committing several thefts, including a July 2022 heist in which approximately $100 million worth of jewelry was stolen from a Brinks semitruck stopped in the Central Valley while it was en route from an international jewelry show in Northern California. Carlos Victor Mestanza Cercado, 33, whose previous addresses include one in Pasadena and who is the lead defendant in this case, pleaded guilty to one count of interference with commerce by robbery (Hobbs Act). Mestanza has been in federal custody since August 2025 after being extradited from Panama, where he had fled upon learning of the criminal charges in this case. According to his plea agreement, from March 2022 to July 2022, Mestanza and other co-conspirators used multiple vehicles to follow truck drivers carrying interstate and foreign shipments to stopping points, including truck stops and other locations where the drivers stopped and their trucks were left unattended. Mestanza and his accomplices then stole the cargo, including by force and threat of force in the presence of the victims. The thieves then returned to Los Angeles County with the stolen merchandise to divide up and sell for profit. In July 2022, a co-conspirator scouted an international jewelry show in San Mateo, communicating by phone with Mestanza and other co-conspirators to steal the jewelry in transit following the show. On July 10, 2022, Mestanza and co-conspirators focused on a Brinks semitruck at the jewelry show that carried 73 bags containing millions of dollars’ worth of jewelry that had traveled in interstate commerce. When the Brinks truck departed, Mestanza and the co-conspirators coordinated by phone and, from the late evening of July 10, 2022, to the early morning of July 11, 2022, followed the truck approximately 300 miles from San Mateo to rest stops in the Central Valley. On July 11, 2022, at a truck stop in Lebec, Mestanza and his accomplices broke the locks on the Brinks truck and stole 24 bags of jewelry, which the victims later valued at approximately $100 million. They then traveled to East Hollywood with the stolen jewelry. In the days that followed, Mestanza and other co-conspirators tried to conceal their identities by deactivating the cellphone numbers they had used to steal the jewelry from the Brinks truck. Mestanza fled the U.S. in June 2025 after a federal grand jury indicted him and several other defendants in connection with the Brinks theft. On July 1, 2025, law enforcement detained Mestanza at Tocumen International Airport in Panama City during a layover from Guatemala to Ecuador. Mestanza further admitted to committing several other thefts with co-conspirators. Specifically, on March 2, 2022, they stole Samsung electronics from a truck at a 7-Eleven store in Ontario, making off with approximately $240,573 in stolen goods that were brought to a co-conspirator’s residence in Los Angeles. On March 11, 2022, Mestanza and others stole Apple AirTags that had traveled from China and were being delivered by truck to a warehouse in Fontana. The truck’s driver had stopped for food when the robbery occurred, and a co-conspirator used a knife to threaten the driver. The thieves made off with approximately $57,377 in stolen goods. Finally, on May 25, 2022, Mestanza and others broke into one truck and stole items from another truck parked at stops in Fontana, stealing approximately $14,081 worth of Samsung electronics. Law enforcement believes that the applicable amount of restitution in this case is at least $100,312,031. United States District Judge Kenly Kiya Kato scheduled an April 15, 2027 sentencing hearing, at which time Mestanza will face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. The following defendants charged in this case have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to go on trial on March 22, 2027: Alberto Javier Loza, 40, a.k.a. “Ricardo Noel Moya, “Ricardo Barbosa,” “Alberto Javier Loza Chamorro,” and “Jazael Padilla Resto,” of Boyle Heights, who is a citizen of Ecuador; Pablo Raul Lugo Larroig, 43, a.k.a. “Walter Loza,” of Rialto, who is a U.S. citizen; and Jorge Enrique Alban, 34, of South Los Angeles, who also is a U.S. citizen. Co-defendants Victor Hugo Valencia Solorzano and Eduardo Macias Ibarra have not appeared in a U.S. courtroom to face the criminal charges against them. On February 12, the charges against Jeson Nelon Presilla Flores, 44, formerly of Upland, were dismissed without prejudice. Presilla, a citizen of Ecuador, has been removed from the United States. The FBI, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, the Fontana Police Department, and the Ontario Police Department are investigating this matter. Assistant United States Attorneys Jena A. MacCabe and Kevin J. Butler of the Major Crimes Section are prosecuting this case. Contact Shawn Lewis Public Affairs Officer shawn.lewis@usdoj.gov (213) 458-6803 Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - California, Central Press Release Number: 26-222

Kansas Realtor Indicted for Tax Evasion, Failure to File Tax Returns, and Pandemic Relief Fraud
body: Press Release Kansas Realtor Indicted for Tax Evasion, Failure to File Tax Returns, and Pandemic Relief Fraud Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs A federal grand jury in Kansas City, Kansas, returned a superseding indictment yesterday charging a Louisburg, Kansas, woman with tax evasion, wire fraud, and willful failure to file personal and corporate income tax returns. According to the superseding indictment, Michelle O’Connor, also known as Michelle Yi Lee, owned and operated a realty company based in the Kansas City metro area. For the years 2008 through 2015, O’Connor allegedly filed federal income tax returns, self-reporting that she owed a total of approximately $300,000 in taxes. According to the superseding indictment, despite reporting to the IRS that she owed taxes, O’Connor did not pay the amounts owed. Starting in 2010, the IRS allegedly began trying to collect the outstanding taxes from O’Connor and sent her a total of more than 50 notices. From 2011 through late 2020, however, O’Connor allegedly stymied the IRS’s collections efforts by, among other things, filing false or frivolous bankruptcy petitions and reducing her bank balances by purchasing more than $250,000 in cashier’s checks to prevent the IRS from levying those accounts. According to the superseding indictment, O’Connor closed some of her personal bank accounts and maintained minimal balances in others in an effort to further obstruct the IRS’s collection efforts. O’Connor also allegedly paid for personal expenses using her business’s bank accounts. By 2020, O’Connor allegedly owed the IRS nearly half a million in taxes, penalties and interest. In 2020, O’Connor also allegedly submitted 34 fraudulent Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) applications on behalf of her real estate business and seven other corporate entities she created for the purpose of applying for these credits. Under the EIDL program, a small business could receive a loan of up to $150,000 from the Small Business Administration to cover six months of working capital. In total, O’Connor allegedly received nearly $300,000 from her fraudulent EIDLs, which she used for personal purposes, including purchasing $115,000 of cryptocurrency. According to the superseding indictment, O’Connor also did not file individual and corporate income tax returns for the years 2020 through 2025 as required by law. O’Connor was charged with one count of tax evasion, two counts of wire fraud, five counts of willful failure to file an individual tax return, and nine counts of willful failure to file a corporate tax return. If convicted, she faces maximum penalties of five years in prison for the tax evasion count, 20 years in prison for each count of wire fraud, and one year in prison for each count of willful failure to file a tax return. She also faces a period of supervised release, restitution and monetary penalties. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser for the District of Kansas made the announcement. IRS Criminal Investigation is investigating the case. Trial Attorneys Dominick Giovanniello and J. Parker Gochenour of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section are prosecuting the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. title: Sacramento man sentenced to 27 years in prison for sexually exploiting a child over Snapchat and Instagram
body: Press Release Sacramento man sentenced to 27 years in prison for sexually exploiting a child over Snapchat and Instagram Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of California SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Francisco Mariano Orantes, 33, of Sacramento, was sentenced today by U.S. District Judge Daniel J. Calabretta to 27 years in prison for sexually exploiting a minor, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced. “For years, this defendant exploited children by gaining their trust through lies and then using coercion and threats to deepen their victimization,” said U.S. Attorney Grant. “Today's sentence reflects the extraordinary harm he inflicted on vulnerable young victims and ensures he will be held accountable for his crimes. The U.S. Attorney's Office remains committed to protecting children from online predators and pursuing redress for victims of exploitation and sextortion.” “There is nothing more important than protecting our children,” said Jim Cooper, Sacramento County Sheriff. “This case highlights countless hours of investigative work by our Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Detectives and law enforcement partners. I could not be more proud of them for hunting down this predator and bringing him to justice.” According to court documents, between 2023 and 2024, Orantes persuaded or coerced at least seven minor female victims to produce sexually explicit images and videos. Using apps like Snapchat and Instagram, Orantes gained his victims’ trust by impersonating a teenage girl and convinced them to trade content. Often, he sent his victims sexually explicit images or videos of the girl he was impersonating and convinced them to produce similar imagery or videos. When his victims would replicate, Orantes would screen record his conversations and download and store the content on his devices. He categorized the images and videos by the child’s name, age or other identifier, in a folder called “Children.” Orantes pleaded guilty on May 21, 2026. One victim told law enforcement that she was coerced into sending Orantes additional material because he found out where she went to school and threatened to tell everyone at school if she did not perform as instructed. In fact, law enforcement later recovered screen recordings showing Orantes using geolocation tools to identify that minor’s address and school, and a saved text file in which he threatened to share the minor’s nude images with people at her school. Another victim similarly reported that Orantes knew her full name and address and threatened to leak her images if she did not comply with his instructions. In total, Orantes was found in possession of more than 11,000 images and more than 14,000 videos of child sexual abuse material on his devices, including images and videos showing the sexual abuse of infants or toddlers. The Internet Crimes Against Children Unit of the Sacramento Valley Hi-Tech Crimes Task Force and the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office conducted the investigation with assistance from the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Dhruv M. Sharma prosecuted the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute those who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC . Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - California, Eastern

title: Shiprock Man Charged with Assault Following Stabbing
body: Press Release Shiprock Man Charged with Assault Following Stabbing Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Mexico ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock man is facing federal charges for allegedly attacking a man with a utility knife at a gas station. According to court documents, on November 11, 2026, Irick Abe Phillips , 49, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, allegedly stabbed a man during an altercation at a gas station in Shiprock, New Mexico. The victim, an employee of the gas station, had asked Phillips to leave the premises when Phillips allegedly threatened him with a utility knife and cut him on the wrist. The victim received treatment at the scene for a laceration to his arm. Court documents allege that after the stabbing, Phillips continued to threaten the victim and attempted to follow him into the gas station while still armed with the knife. Employees locked the doors to prevent Phillips from entering. Phillips was eventually disarmed and detained by the victim and bystanders until law enforcement arrived. Law enforcement officers recovered a knife believed to have been used in the assault. Investigators also reviewed surveillance footage that corroborated witness accounts of the incident. Phillips is charged with assault with a dangerous weapon. He will remain in custody pending  trial, which has not been scheduled. If convicted of the current charge, Phillips faces up to 10 years in prison. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today. The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Nation Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jack Burkhead is prosecuting the case. A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. title: Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty to Unlawful Reentry
body: Press Release Illegal Alien Pleads Guilty to Unlawful Reentry Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Massachusetts BOSTON – A Brazilian national who recently completed a two-year sentence in the Middlesex House of Correction for Operating Under the Influence (4th or greater offense) pleaded guilty yesterday in federal court in Boston to unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation. Jose Antonio Ramos, 52, pleaded guilty to one count of unlawful reentry of a deported alien before U.S. Senior District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV who scheduled sentencing for Feb. 17, 2027. Ramos was indicted by a federal grand jury in April 2026 . According to the charging documents, the defendant was removed from the United States on two occasions, once in 2006 and a second time in November 2008. After each removal, he reentered the United States at unknown dates and unknown places without being inspected or admitted by an immigration officer. The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Suzanne Sullivan Jacobus of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case. Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Massachusetts

title: 13 Defendants Arrested on Federal Indictment Charging Them With Stealing More Than $22.5 Million in Consumer Goods from Trains
body: Press Release 13 Defendants Arrested on Federal Indictment Charging Them With Stealing More Than $22.5 Million in Consumer Goods from Trains Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California LOS ANGELES – 13 defendants were arrested today on a 17-count federal indictment charging them with burglarizing at least three dozen trains and stealing more than $22 million worth of Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, and other products, then selling them on the black market, coordinating their thefts via Instagram. “The scale of the theft is staggering. We have charged a crew of 14 in a scheme to steal more than $22.5 million in cargo from at least three dozen freight trains in Southern California,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash.” “This historic indictment, following a 14-month investigation assisted by our Bureau of Investigation, demonstrates the importance of dismantling entire criminal enterprises — from those stealing the cargo to those profiting from its resale,” Los Angeles County Nathan J. Hochman said. “We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market.” The following defendants charged today are expected to make their initial appearances and be arraigned on the indictment this afternoon in United States District Court in downtown Los Angeles: Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, the crew’s leader; Daniel Angel, 38, a.k.a. “Rayo,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s father; Rodolfo Angel, 23, a.k.a. “Rudy” and “Flaco,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s uncle; Jose Luis Angel, 23, a.k.a. “Joe,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s uncle; Donta Hedgeman, 27, a.k.a. “Dret,” of East Los Angeles; Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, of the Historic South-Central neighborhood of Los Angeles; Daniel Garcia, 36, of East Los Angeles; Carlos Robert Estrada, 28, a.k.a. “JD,” of Whittier; Angel Sanchez, 24, a.k.a. “Fluffy,” of Commerce; Ruben Mario Banuelos, 26, a.k.a. “Bubu,” of East Los Angeles; Fredy Marquina, 25, of the Westlake neighborhood of Los Angeles; Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, of the Vermont Square area of South Los Angeles; Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, of East Los Angeles; Ricardo Mares, 32, of the Florence-Firestone area of Los Angeles. The federal grand jury charged all 14 defendants with one count of conspiracy. The indictment further charges 14 counts of theft of interstate railroad cargo and possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and two counts of violence against railroad carriers. According to the indictment, shipping containers with Nike sneakers and other freight routinely enter the United States from international destinations via the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach then are transported by trains operated by carrier companies for further distribution throughout the U.S. From February 2024 to August 2026, Nathan Angel targeted high-value trains traveling through Southern California carrying Nike sneakers and other products, intending to steal them and resell them on the black market. At his direction, Daniel Angel, Rodolfo Angel, Jose Angel, Villegas, Estrada, and Sanchez rented or used trucks and vans to drive burglars to the railroad tracks, where the burglars boarded the trains. These co-defendants also acted as lookouts. Nathan Angel and other co-conspirators pre-determined locations along the tracks to disable the trains. Hedgeman and other co-conspirators then cut the air hoses of the trains, forcing the trains to come to an emergency stop. Daniel Angel, Rodolfo Angel, Jose Angel, Villegas, Estrada, and Sanchez met the train burglars where they had disabled the trains and helped load stolen train cargo into trucks and vans, which they then transported to stash houses, including the residences of Villegas, Garcia, and Daniel Angel. The burglaries occurred on railroad tracks in Pico Rivera, Fullerton, and other locations in Southern California. Nathan Angel alerted Garcia about the type of products that had been stolen from the trains. They would then discuss resale prices for the stolen products. Nathan Angel sent to Marquina, Martinez, and Espinoza photographs of the stolen Nike sneakers and other products, often while the trains were being burglarized. These co-defendants knowingly took the stolen products into their possession. Marquina then contacted potential buyers, including representatives of a business identified in the indictment as  “Company 1,” a sneaker and streetwear resale brand with headquarters in Los Angeles that was not an authorized Nike reseller. Marquina and Martinez sold the stolen Nike sneakers and other products to Company 1, which then sold the stolen products for a profit. From May 2025 to October 2025, Marquina and Martinez sold thousands of pairs of stolen Nike sneakers, many in their original Nike factory cartons, to Company 1 and received from Company 1 a total of approximately $1,081,493 for the stolen Nike products and other stolen items. Espinoza also obtained stolen Nike sneakers and other stolen goods from suppliers, including Nathan Angel. Garcia helped deliver the stolen goods to Espinoza’s residence, where Espinoza stored them. Espinoza advertised the stolen goods to potential buyers, including on social media accounts. He then sold the stolen goods to buyers for a profit. An indictment contains allegations that a defendant has committed a crime. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent until and unless proven guilty in court. If convicted, the defendants would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for the conspiracy count, up to 10 years in federal prison for each theft count, and a statutory maximum sentence of life in federal prison for each violence against railroad cars count. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Los Angeles Police Department Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department, and the California Highway Patrol Cargo Theft Interdiction Program, with assistance from IRS Criminal Investigation, are investigating this matter. Assistant United States Attorney Diane Roldán and Eric Mackie of the Major Crimes Section is prosecuting this case, with assistance from the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office. Contact Shawn Lewis Public Affairs Officer shawn.lewis@usdoj.gov (213) 458-6803 Updated November 19, 2026 Component USAO - California, Central Press Release Number: 26-221

title: Norway Man Pleads Guilty to Burglarizing a Gun Store and Illegally Possessing Firearms
body: Press Release Norway Man Pleads Guilty to Burglarizing a Gun Store and Illegally Possessing Firearms Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maine Grover Lee Harmon stole 12 firearms PORTLAND, Maine: A Norway man pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in Portland to stealing firearms from a federally licensed firearms dealer and being a felon in possession of a firearm. According to court records, in March 2026, 12 handguns were stolen from J&K Sporting Goods in West Paris, a federally licensed firearms dealer. In April 2026, Grover Lee Harmon , 41, was arrested on unrelated warrants during a traffic stop. A search of Harmon’s vehicle revealed three pistol magazines. Investigators subsequently executed a search warrant at a residence used by Harmon and his girlfriend and located two of the firearms stolen in the March burglary. During an interview with investigators, Harmon admitted to being part of the gun store burglary, and acknowledged he handled the firearms after they were taken from the store. Harmon is prohibited from possessing firearms as a result of a prior felony conviction. For the theft charge, Harmon faces up to five years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and a maximum supervised release term of three years. For the illegal possession of a firearm charge, Harmon faces up to 15 years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and a maximum supervised release term of three years. He will be sentenced after the completion of a presentence investigative report by the U.S. Probation Office. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case with the assistance of the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office, the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office, and the Norway Police Department. Operation Take Back America: This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN). ### Contact Peter I. Brostowin, Assistant United States Attorney (Tel: 207-780-3257) Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Operation Take Back America Components Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) USAO - Maine

title: Kansas City Attorney and His Client Sentenced to Probation with Intermittent Confinement in a Local Facility
body: Press Release Kansas City Attorney and His Client Sentenced to Probation with Intermittent Confinement in a Local Facility Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Missouri KANSAS CITY, Mo. –Two Kansas City men have been sentenced in federal court following their convictions for criminal contempt earlier this year. Charles Floyd Anderson, 82, and his attorney Robert Pete Smith, 81, were sentenced by U.S. District Judge Roseann Ketchmark to five years of probation. As part of these sentences of probation, the court also imposed a special condition which requires Smith to serve four weeks of intermittent confinement and Anderson to serve four days of intermittent confinement at a facility designated by the U.S. Marshal Service. Smith and Anderson are also required to surrender their passports and remain within the jurisdiction of the Western District of Missouri, and Johnson County, Kansas and Wyandotte County, Kansas, unless granted permission to leave by the court, for the duration of their probation sentences. Smith was ordered to serve his intermittent confinement on Monday, Nov. 30, 2026, through the morning of Dec. 28, 2026. Anderson was also ordered to serve intermittent confinement on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, through Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026. Smith and Anderson were found guilty of contempt by U.S. District Judge Roseann Ketchmark on March 16, 2026. The Court found Anderson and Smith willfully violated a court order to provide truthful, accurate and complete financial disclosures in an underlying civil action. The civil action was brought by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the State of Missouri alleging that consumers paid over $100 million in response to deceptive sweepstakes and prize mailers distributed by a family business enterprise built by Anderson, FTC v. Next-Gen, Inc. et al. , No. 18-cv-00128-DGK (FTC Case). Smith, a then partner at McDowell Rice Smith & Buchanan, P.C., represented Anderson and his businesses for over 25 years before the FTC Case. As part of the FTC case, Anderson was ordered to complete certain individual and corporate financial disclosures. The entities, accounts and transactions that supported the criminal contempt proceeding involved Anderson and Smith acting as business partners or close friends, reaching far outside of the typical attorney-client relationship. The criminal contempt case focused on the apparent effort undertaken by Smith to conceal that affiliation and wash himself and his business relationship with Anderson from the FTC disclosures. Anderson, as a lay person, had a duty to provide truthful, accurate and complete information to the FTC. Following the bench trial, the Court found, “Attorney Smith and Anderson willfully violated both the letter and the spirit of the financial disclosure required by the district court in the FTC Case. . . . Orders duly entered by a district court must be followed and respected. Persons or parties who do not do so, and who instead opt for willful deceptive gamesmanship or otherwise act in bad faith in complying with a district court’s orders are subject to criminal sanction.” The Court further found that “Defendants’ conduct illustrates a picture of deception and sanitization of particular relationships and assets from the FTC’s view.” The Court ultimately adjudged Anderson and Smith guilty of criminal contempt as charged. This case was being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Patrick D. Daly and Matthew N. Sparks and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda K. Hanson. It was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Fraud Component USAO - Missouri, Western

body: Press Release Knox Place Traffickers Sentenced in Narcotics Conspiracy that Reached from Southern California to Southeast D.C. Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia WASHINGTON – Reginald Lassiter, 40, of the District of Columbia; Terrance Lynwood Boyd, 44, of Capitol Heights, Maryland; and Michael Anderson Thomas, 50, of Chino, California, were sentenced in U.S. District Court in connection with their roles in a drug trafficking organization that distributed fentanyl, PCP, heroin, and cocaine in Southeast Washington, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. “This conspiracy crossed neighborhoods, state lines, and every boundary the defendants thought would shield them from accountability,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “From a California shell company used to funnel drug proceeds, to stash houses in Baltimore, to the streets of Southeast Washington, every piece of the operation left evidence behind. This case sends a clear message: those who flood our streets with dangerous drugs will be held accountable, prosecuted, and sent to prison.” Lassiter, aka "Lip," pleaded guilty on June 17 before U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly to conspiracy to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl. On November 10, Judge Kelly sentenced Lassister to a 120-month prison term and ordered Lassiter to serve five years of supervised release. Boyd pleaded guilty on June 12, 2026, before Judge Kelly to possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense. On November 17, Judge Kelly sentenced Boyd to a 60-month prison term and ordered Boyd to serve five years of supervised release. Thomas pleaded guilty on July 22, 2026, before Judge Kelly to conspiracy to distribute one kilogram or more of phencyclidine (PCP) and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. On November 19, Judge Kelly sentenced Thomas to 195 months in prison and ordered him to serve five years of supervised release. According to court documents, in the summer of 2024, FBI agents initiated a long-term investigation of a drug trafficking conspiracy centered around the 2900 block of Knox Place, SE. Law enforcement had identified an alleged fentanyl and PCP trafficker in the 2900 block of Knox Place. As the investigation progressed, law enforcement identified upstream sources of supply for both narcotics, including California-based co-conspirators such as Thomas. During the conspiracy, five homicides, seventeen assaults with dangerous weapons, five robberies and eight burglaries occurred within 1,000 feet of the conspiracy's primary stash location on Knox Place SE, court papers state. The investigation culminated in August 2025 when law enforcement executed 20 residential search warrants across the District of Columbia, Maryland, and Los Angeles and arrested fourteen individuals. Investigators seized 20 firearms, large quantities of fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and PCP, a kilo press used to compact narcotics, and more than $100,000 in cash. Lassiter operated as a fentanyl supplier within the conspiracy. He served as an intermediary between the conspiracy’s Baltimore-based bulk fentanyl supplier, Thomas Hancock, and the street-level supplier in the 2900 block of Knox Place, co-defendant Eric Prather. Lassiter and Prather maintained a stash house within the 2900 block of Knox Place, which they used to both store and distribute fentanyl and other narcotics. The lavender-hued fentanyl called “purple rain,” that Lassiter supplied to a co-conspirator Feb. 11, 2025. Boyd possessed firearms in furtherance of the organization's drug trafficking activities. During a Aug. 26, 2025, search of a residence on the 2900 block of Knox Place SE, agents recovered a Draco-style firearm from a backpack stashed inside a bedroom closet. Nearby, they recovered distribution quantities of fentanyl, PCP, and heroin. DNA analysis linked Boyd to the firearm. Later that day, agents searched Boyd's residence in the 1200 block of Southern Avenue SE, where they recovered more than $10,000 in cash and a loaded Ruger 5.7 pistol. During a Aug. 26, 2025, search of a residence on the 2900 block of Knox Place SE agents recovered a Draco-style firearm from a backpack stashed inside a bedroom closet. Nearby, they recovered distribution quantities of fentanyl, PCP, and heroin. Thomas facilitated bulk shipments of PCP to co-conspirators operating in the Baltimore-Washington region from his operating base in Chino, California. In late-2024, he agreed to ship 17 gallons of PCP to Hancock. To accept payments for his drug trafficking, Thomas created a California shell company, Never to Late Shipping LLC. Between August 2024 and March 2025, he accepted about $170,000 through the company in connection with the PCP transaction with Hancock. In March 2025, Thomas’ business partner, Darrell Smith, was stopped by Kansas state police outside of Topeka. Kansas state police subsequently conducted a search of Smith’s Dodge Ram and found approximately 17 gallons of PCP concealed within a black lockbox in the truck bed. The PCP was packaged in 17 one-gallon cans that were each sealed. The PCP was packaged in 17 sealed one-gallon cans. Approximately five months later, Thomas’ residence in Chino, California, was searched as part of the coordinated search and arrest operation in this case. In the rear of the residence, a standalone backyard shed serving as a clandestine PCP laboratory was located, containing chemical production materials, multiple large-capacity trash bins and other paraphernalia, including a Senior Master Can Sealer Model 1502. Law enforcement separately located $26,000 in cash and two loaded handguns within the residence, each of which Thomas admitted to possessing. Investigators uncovered a clandestine PCP lab in a shed in Thomas’ backyard in Chino, California. The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office, with valuable assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration, Washington Division Office, and the Metropolitan Police Department. The matter was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Matthew W. Kinskey and John Crabb, Jr., of the Violent Crime and Narcotics Trafficking Section. This operation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by President Trump’s Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Washington D.C. comprises agents and officers from the FBI, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Drug Enforcement Administration, Homeland Security Investigations, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, IRS Criminal Investigations and others with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. 25cr241 25cr273 Follow us on X , Instagram , and YouTube Or at https://www.justice.gov/usao-dc Updated November 19, 2026 Topics Homeland Security Task Force Drug Trafficking Components Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - District of Columbia

title: Former Sheriff’s Deputy, Wife Admit Trying to Coerce Teen into Sexual Activity
body: Press Release Former Sheriff’s Deputy, Wife Admit Trying to Coerce Teen into Sexual Activity Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Missouri ST. LOUIS – A former deputy sheriff and his wife, a former 911 dispatcher, have admitted trying to coerce a child into engaging in sexual activity. David Blankenship, 41, of St. Francois County, pleaded guilty Thursday in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of attempted coercion and enticement of a child. His wife, Karlie Blankenship, 31, pleaded guilty in August to the same charge. The couple both admitted spending months planning how to get an 11-year-old to engage in sex with them. In TikTok and Facebook exchanges beginning in February 2024, the two discussed their desire to meet and have sexual relationships with underage girls. David Blankenship sent his wife pictures of local girls that he’d found online and told her to connect with them. He suggested exchanging drugs for sex with them. The couple also discussed producing and selling pornography online. When their attention turned to the 11-year-old, David Blankenship discussed drugging her with muscle relaxers or hallucinogenic mushrooms and bought her a sex toy. Karlie Blankenship showed the victim images of teenage girls in erotic clothing to gauge her interest. The investigation began when the Missouri State Highway Patrol received a CyberTip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) about the uploading of files that contained suspected child sexual abuse material, and a warning that the suspect "may be law enforcement at St. Francois County Sheriff’s Department and may have current ACCESS TO CHILDREN." Investigators then uncovered the social media communications. When they conducted a court-approved search of the Blankenship home, they found the sex toy, mushrooms in a bag in the Blankenships’ bedroom and methamphetamine in the pocket of a pair of pants worn by David Blankenship. David Blankenship’s employment with the St. Francois County Sheriff’s Department was terminated when his department learned of the allegations. Karlie Blankenship is scheduled to be sentenced on December 1 and David Blankenship on February 17. The charge carries a mandatory minimum prison term of 10 years and a maximum term of life. The Missouri State Highway Patrol, the Missouri State Technical Assistance Team and the St. Francois County Sheriff’s Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Hayes is prosecuting the case. Contact Robert Patrick, Public Affairs Officer, robert.patrick@usdoj.gov. Updated November 19, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Missouri, Eastern
