title: Google’s water stewardship commitments for local communities
body: Google’s water stewardship commitments for local communities Nov 19, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Learn about our water commitments and initiatives. Ben Townsend Head of Infrastructure & Sustainability Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Data centers are the nerve centers of the digital world, powering our daily lives with Search, Maps, online banking, healthcare and 911 systems. As we grow our data center footprint to support these services, we recognize that how we build is just as important as what we build. Water is a critical component of data center development and operations. Because data centers generate heat from the servers and chips that power the digital world, they often rely on water to cut back on energy use for cooling. In many places, water cooling can reduce data center energy use by approximately 10% compared to air cooling. The aggregate water consumption of data centers is small — U.S. data centers use less than 1% of the water that Americans use on their lawns annually 1 — but we are focused on protecting local water resources in all aspects of our data center operations. We are committed to responsibly manage vital water resources where we build and operate data centers. Our goal is to minimize our local impacts so that our growth does not come at the expense of the communities we call home. We’re also announcing new water stewardship initiatives and evaluating projects through Google’s water replenishment Request for Information (RFI). New water stewardship commitments Under these five commitments, Google will: Replenish more water than we consume at our sites 2 by 2030. By investing in replenishment projects, we can help improve water security for everyone. In 2025, we replenished more than 7 billion gallons (roughly equivalent to the annual water usage of 70,000 average U.S. households). 3 And, as of 2025, we have 165 water stewardship projects across 97 watersheds . Once these projects are fully implemented, they are expected to replenish more than 19 billion gallons of water annually by 2030, more than double our 2024 consumption (enough water to supply the entire city of Los Angeles for more than 40 days). The majority of these projects not only deliver volumetric benefits, but also help improve broader watershed health challenges such as water quality. Help modernize water and wastewater infrastructure for our neighbors. Water utilities are often underfunded. By working with our utility partners, we are helping update public water infrastructure so that our neighbors have reliable, affordable water sources both today and in the future. In addition to paying for the water we use, to date Google has committed over $500 million to the development of water, wastewater and water reuse infrastructure and to the utility partners that deliver water in the communities where we operate/build data centers. This includes projects ranging from enhancing local water supplies to detecting leaky pipes . We’re committed to continuing to help local utilities update their infrastructure. Protect at-risk watersheds with air-cooled solutions. We use a data-driven framework to assess local watersheds for new data centers before we build, and only consider water cooling if local resources are healthy and resilient. If a water source is at high risk, we choose air cooling or recycled water. We will continue to work in partnership with state agencies and local utilities to follow these principles and ensure our approach reflects community needs. Report our annual water use transparently. Water use shouldn’t be a “black box.” Google was the first major cloud provider to disclose our annual water use for our data center locations, and we’re committed to continuing to do so to ensure transparency for the communities where we invest and build. Pursue alternative and reclaimed solutions to protect water resources. We are working with utility partners to identify freshwater alternatives at our data centers, such as reclaimed wastewater. A prime example is in Douglas County, Georgia , where we partnered with the county’s water and sewer authority to reuse treated wastewater for cooling at our data center campus. Google’s water replenishment RFI To further our replenishment goals, we’re also evaluating more than 700 projects submitted through our recent Water Replenishment Projects RFI . These projects include engineered solutions to improve water efficiency, supply or quality; farm-level practices to reduce agricultural water demand and improve soil health; and nature-based solutions aimed at improving the hydrologic cycle. We’ll have more to share in the coming months as we work with partners to roll out these projects. Water is an essential natural resource that communities work hard to conserve. Through our water stewardship commitments, we will continue to be responsible and transparent in our water use — protecting the long-term health of the watersheds in communities we call home. New water stewardship initiatives Last updated: November 19, 2026 Our commitment to water stewardship has grown significantly. This year, we've announced over $100 million in funding to support community water sources, infrastructure, and access in 14 states. Here’s a list of our latest water stewardship initiatives, and we’ll be updating this list on an ongoing basis. Arkansas: Ducks Unlimited to support key park amenities at Ducks Unlimited Park, bringing learning and interactive program opportunities to children and other park visitors across the Mid-South. Arizona: Trout Unlimited and the US Fish and Wildlife Service to remove and replace culverts that will restore natural streamflow and reconnect vital habitats for the Apache Trout. Georgia: Ducks Unlimited to enhance wetlands at the Flint River Wildlife Management Area. Indiana: Fort Wayne City Utilities to optimize water reuse at its water treatment plant, reducing withdrawals from the St. Joseph River. Iowa: The Great Outdoors Foundation and the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship to help local farmers in Western Iowa convert 5,000 acres into perennial hay and pasture systems, reducing fertilizer use and improving water quality. Bur Oak Land Trust to acquire and convert a 165-acre property adjacent to the Corriell Nature Preserve into managed wetlands and prairies to enhance natural infiltration and recharge. Michigan: Huron River Watershed Council to expand its green infrastructure program, using native plantings to treat stormwater and mitigate flooding. Minnesota: Trust for Public Land to restore 84 acres of floodplain forest, establishing a 1-mile corridor along the Zumbro River to improve water quality. Missouri: Bridging the Gap and the Heartland Conservation Alliance to restore 98 acres adjacent to the Blue River as a wetland, improving water quality and providing critical habitat. Nebraska: The Metropolitan Utilities District’s water line leak detection program in Omaha to help reduce water loss and improve system efficiency. Ohio: Department of Agriculture’s H2Ohio Farmland Water Management Program to optimize drainage structures to reduce agricultural runoff and conserve water. Oklahoma: Oklahoma Conservation Commission to remove invasive, water-intensive Eastern Red Cedar trees and restore cropland to native playa wetlands in the panhandle. South Carolina: National Audubon Society to construct nature-based features, specifically berms, that will protect wetlands and their corresponding habitat in the Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. Texas: Funding to support community water sources, infrastructure, and access across the state. Virginia: Frog Creek Partners to improve water quality throughout Virginia’s Chesapeake Bay and Roanoke River watersheds by installing stormwater filtration systems. The Virginia Association of Soil and Water Conservation Districts (VASWCD) to reduce the quantity and improve the water quality of stormwater runoff entering natural waterways across public, private, and Tribal lands. Ducks Unlimited to support the enhancement of approximately 60 acres of wetlands at the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources James River and Dick Cross Wildlife Management Areas, as well as support the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s efforts in restoring tidal, freshwater wetland dynamics within the Elizabeth Hartwell Mason Neck National Wildlife Refuge. ION Water to support the deployment of their End-to-End Water Management system across approximately 4,500 affordable housing units in Northern Virginia and the Metro DC area. title: Cyber resilience guidance consultation and AI and quantum effective practices
body:
Cyber resilience guidance consultation and AI and quantum effective practices | Bank of England – the UK's central bank Our use of cookies We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Cyber resilience guidance consultation and AI and quantum effective practices UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. Published on  
        19 November 2026 News release UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. The Bank of England’s (the Bank) latest Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in 5 years, 52% above the previous 18-month peak recorded in May 2025. In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them. The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast evolving threat environment. It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers. Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: 'Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance. 'Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.' Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said: 'Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.' Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said: 'We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents. 'The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.' Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area. Notes to editors The consultation closes on 26 February 2027. Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year. The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements. The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve. The proposed guidance covers key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas including: - Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management , with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate Board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance. - Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk , maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts. - Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats , applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains. - Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly , through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks. - Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively , with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned. The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future. See Effective practices: Cyber risk and resilience management relating to artificial intelligence (AI) and Effective practices: Cyber risk and resilience management relating to quantum computing . A recent Bank of England and FCA survey , found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years. In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI. title: Minutes of the Market Participants Group meeting – 18 November 2026
body:
Minutes of the Market Participants Group meeting – 18 November 2026 | Bank of England – the UK's central bank Our use of cookies We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. By clicking ‘Accept recommended settings’ on this banner, you accept our use of analytics cookies.   For more information on how these cookies work please see our Cookie policy . Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Minutes of the Market Participants Group meeting – 18 November 2026 The Market Participants Group (MPG) is a senior-level forum for financial market participants to share their views on relevant themes and narratives in financial markets with members of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee. Published on  
        19 November 2026 Time: 5pm – 6.30pm | Location: Bank of England Published on 19 November 2026 Minutes Item 1 – Welcome The Governor began the meeting by thanking attendees for joining and reminding participants of the purpose of these meetings. The Governor made clear that the MPC would be in listening mode, and that the meeting would be conducted in accordance with relevant competition and conduct laws, as per the terms of reference . Item 2 – International developments Market participants opened by discussing developments in major advanced economies outside the UK. The resilience of global growth and the strength of corporate sector balance sheets, particularly in the United States, were noted. Energy markets were also discussed, with market participants highlighting the inherent difficulty of forecasting energy prices amid continued geopolitical uncertainty. The material support to global growth from AI-related capital expenditure was noted. Participants also discussed the increasing role of debt financing and the potential implications of a change in expectations around AI for risky asset markets, investment and consumption. The discussion also covered potential financial market vulnerabilities arising from elevated hedge-fund leverage, sovereign debt pressures and cyber risks. Item 3 – Domestic developments Market participants discussed the outlook for the UK economy and the implications for monetary policy. Participants noted the resilience of UK growth this year despite the energy shock. This resilience was broadly seen to have strengthened the case for higher rates, with the November increase having been widely expected. Growth in global AI-related investment was noted as one factor supporting UK activity, although there was some discussion over the extent to which the resilience in domestic growth would persist. Participants also discussed the implications of AI-related growth for domestic inflationary pressure. Market participants noted the correlation between energy prices and market rates, and how this relationship had evolved over recent months. In discussing the implications of the energy shock, views differed on the relative importance of its demand and supply-side effects. The distinction between implied pricing in the market curve and modal expectations for policy was also noted by market participants. Attendees Market Participants Group (MPG) members Johanna Kyrklund – Schroders Andrew Law – Caxton Associates LLP Fraser Lundie – Aviva Investors Kunal Shah – Goldman Sachs Pranav Thakur – JP Morgan Gertjan Vlieghe – Millennium Capital Partners Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) members Andrew Bailey Sarah Breeden Megan Greene Catherine L Mann Huw Pill Dave Ramsden Alan Taylor Bank of England staff Geoff Coppins Michael Foster Lydia Henning Victoria Saporta Fergal Shortall Convert this page to PDF Other news News // News release 19 November 2026 Cyber resilience guidance consultation and... title: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon
body: Introducing Gemini 4 Neon Nov 18, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion  across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link In this article Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on: Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science. Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models. For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card . Built for deeper analysis In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs. Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data. Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund. Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently. Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio. For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity. For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app . For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team. body:

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 18, 2026 Investing in America’s Underserved Communities Governor Michael S. Barr At Making Missing Markets: Catalyzing Capital and Igniting Innovation, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York Share Thank you to the New York Fed and the organizers of this conference for the opportunity to speak to you today. 1 For two reasons I can think of, New York is an excellent place to discuss ways to increase investments in communities where incomplete or missing markets have resulted in less investment than needed. First, it makes sense to initiate a conversation about incentivizing private investment in the center of American finance. Second, New York has been successful over the past few decades in attracting investment in lower-income neighborhoods, reversing forces that once made parts of this city synonymous with urban decline. I first saw that for myself 30 years ago, touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public–private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer, block by block. That progress has continued, and the strategies and partnerships we will be discussing today have been a major engine for that success. The backdrop for community investment, of course, is the economy—how fast it is growing, how well it is creating jobs, and how well incomes are keeping up with the cost of living. So I will start with the economic outlook. Overall, the economy is strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment. But inflation is too high, making it hard for American families to make ends meet. Many families are struggling. And that's why it is so important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to our target of 2 percent in a timely way. If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people. Of course, I'll continue to monitor the incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks in making that assessment. Strong and sustainable communities are key to American prosperity. When a community is strong and resilient, people see a future there and invest in that future—they buy homes, shop locally, and start new businesses. When hard times hit resilient communities, people can weather the storm and bounce back in part because they believe that they and their communities will bounce back—that jobs and opportunities will return. That's why we at the Fed are committed to building stronger communities. And while economic activity and employment are continuing to grow for the country as a whole, not all families and communities are thriving. Far from it. Wealthier households are doing well, but middle- and lower-income households are struggling, and the economy is leaving some communities behind. Recent estimates are that 44 percent of Americans live in low-income communities, where a fifth or more of people live below the poverty line. 2 These communities often lack sufficient investment in housing, business, and infrastructure. The Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that the majority of households has very little wealth. 3 And lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say that they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help or provide that help themselves. 4 Think about how that inability to help, or get help, can reverberate across a community. When jobs and opportunities lag in a community, it eats away at the ties that connect families and neighbors. The dignity of work is so key to how many people try to navigate these difficult times, yet in many communities, despite a strong economy, some people are finding it hard to find a good-paying job. So, what are the kinds of investments that can drive long-term, lasting opportunity? We've seen so many examples of successful public–private partnerships make a difference to households, businesses, and communities. We need the public sector, at all levels of government. We need the private sector. And we need the nonprofit sector. But there are market failures that often prevent the private sector from coming in on its own. For example, information asymmetries can make it hard for commercial banks to see opportunities in low-income areas. When commercial banks can partner with local, state, and national community development groups, including Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), that partnership can help those banks extend credit, investment, and services to those that most need them and, in turn, assist banks in most effectively reaching new customers. These partnerships can help overcome these market failures. Community organizations and national nonprofits can reduce the costs of acquiring and interpreting information about low-income borrowers and communities, they can coordinate lending to overcome collective action problems, and they can also share risks to reduce bank exposures. By targeting investments to identify root causes of the challenges in a community, public–private partnerships can better help capital find successful strategies at the early stages of the development process. This can help establish the appropriate funding infrastructure to set community-focused projects on a course for long-term investment. 5 As President John Williams said in inaugurating this conference in 2024, this event is about investing in solutions that lead to long-term partnerships and sustainable success. 6 It means addressing root causes, and also the longer-term outlook for the community. Investments that focus on jobs, housing, schools, infrastructure, and the like are critical. To illustrate what I mean, I will note a few examples of where communities in the region are building partnerships to attract long-term investments. Not far from here, in a part of Brooklyn marked by limited housing as well as a lack of employment and healthy food sources, private and public partners came together in a project called City Point, which includes a full-service supermarket, 120 affordable housing units, and retail space for local small businesses. City Point is a great example of how the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) can leverage private investment into communities and spur further development. 7 I helped launch the bipartisan NMTC a quarter century ago, and I'm so pleased that it was recently made permanent by Congress. In Middletown, New York, the city is converting a historic railway station, long vacant, into a community center, complete with a Head Start program in a community where childcare options are sparse. The project is being financed in part by the NMTC. Syracuse, New York, announced earlier this year the creation of a revolving loan fund for mixed-income housing. The fund provided $30 million in seed money, and a group of private partners contributed the remaining $120 million. The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LITHC) has been a critical tool so important to the recovery of the Bronx and many communities around the country. The LIHTC has helped to create or preserve nearly 4 million units of housing over the past 40 years. 8 The Bronx lost roughly a fifth of its housing between 1970 and 1980 and, not coincidentally, about a fifth of its population. But with the help of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), the LIHTC, CDFIs, and other factors, it recovered that ground and continues to recover and thrive since then. 9 Underpinning all of these projects is the CRA. The CRA has helped to increase lending, investment, and services in low-income communities all across the country. Critical to the CRA's success are banks of all sizes—the biggest banks that serve national markets, regional banks, banks with specialized business models, and community banks—in all kinds of communities, including urban, suburban, small towns, and rural. Banks large and small often partner with CDFIs, national and local community as well as civil rights groups, local chambers of commerce, and the like to make local lending effective. CDFIs are often "boots on the ground" financial providers and can connect stakeholders across sectors. Grants to these and other groups often make the difference between success and failure for banks trying to make a difference in communities—as I said, in rural communities, small towns, big cities, and Native American lands alike. Today, I've spoken mostly about community development in New York, since we're here in the Second District, but I've seen work like this first-hand all around the country as I've visited the Reserve Bank Districts. I've listened to bankers, CDFIs, and local entrepreneurs come together in Clarksdale, Mississippi. I've seen affordable housing built by partnerships between tribal governments and local banks on the Flathead and Blackfeet Reservations in Montana. I've seen Working Cities in East Harford, Connecticut, and community-based learning in Portland, Oregon. I've witnessed the transformation, innovation, and entrepreneurial spirit of Detroit, Michigan, and the grit and determination of community development professionals in South Dallas, Texas. Entrepreneurs in Charlotte, North Carolina, told me about the importance of CDFIs, as did leaders in Kansas City, Missouri, and Omaha, Nebraska. I've seen what public–private partnerships mean for employment and small business growth in Cleveland, Ohio, and I've seen a business incubator in Atlanta, Georgia, make a real difference to its local community. In Arizona, I visited with entrepreneurs in Mesa and Tempe who told us about the key role of local community development corporations. And Chicago educational leaders taught me the importance of linking up with local employers to chart job pathways for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds. This good work is happening all over the country, in urban, rural, and tribal communities, and in every Reserve Bank District. This brings us to why we are gathered today at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In one part of this building, staff are working every day to help implement monetary policy, help ensure smooth financial markets, and promote a strong economy. But we can't achieve a strong economy without strong communities. Core to the Fed's mission, the Federal Reserve System's Community Development function can help. I applaud the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for bringing attention to the untapped potential of low- and moderate-income communities all across these beautiful, vast, diverse, and entrepreneurial United States. There's lots more we can do together. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. See Tracy Hadden Loh, Lyneir Richardson, and Bethany Krupicka, " The Community Investment Fund: An Efficient, Scalable Vehicle for Tax-Incentivized Place-Based Investment ," Brookings, April 16, 2025. Return to text 3. More information on the Survey of Consumer Finances is available on the Board's website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm . Return to text 4. See Aditya Aladangady, Jesse Bricker, Andrew C. Chang, Sarena Goodman, and Gina Li, " Informal Support Networks in the Survey of Consumer Finances ," FEDS Notes (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, October 9, 2026). Return to text 5. See, for example, Michael S. Barr, " Developing Communities through Public-Private Partnerships ," speech delivered at the 2026 National Community Investment Conference, Phoenix, Arizona, March 24, 2026. Return to text 6. See John C. Williams, " X Marks the Spot: Making Missing Markets ," speech delivered at Intermediating Impact: Making Missing Markets, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York City, November 14, 2024. Return to text 7. See Michael S. Barr, " Supporting Investment in Communities: The First 25 Years of the New Markets Tax Credit ," speech delivered at the 2025 Fall New Markets Tax Credit Conference, New Orleans, Louisiana, October 23, 2025. Return to text 8. See "Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) Program: Property Level Data" on the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's Office of Policy Development and Research HUD User website at https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/lihtc/property.html . Return to text 9. See Benjamin Holtzman, " The Burning of the Bronx: Reconstructing a Decade of Abandonment, Arson, and Reform ," Metropolitics, May 26, 2026; and Office of the New York State Comptroller, The South Bronx: An Economic Snapshot (PDF) , Report 13-2024 (Albany, N.Y.: OSC, November 2023). title: Google for Mexico: Technology impact that goes beyond business
body: Google for Mexico: Technology impact that goes beyond business Nov 18, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link At this year’s Google for Mexico, we announced how our latest AI innovations and partnerships are translating into real-world growth across the country. Sebastian Valverde Country Managing Director, Google Mexico Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary Sebastian Valverde, Country Managing Director for Google Mexico, reports that our tools contributed 382 billion pesos to the local economy in 2025. We are now launching a Gemini app for low-memory Android devices to provide students and business owners with better access to digital tools. You can visit our website to read the full Economic Impact Report and learn more about our ongoing partnerships with local institutions. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Sebastian Valverde reports that Google tools contributed 382 billion pesos to the Mexican economy during 2025. We are partnering with national agencies to provide precise weather alerts for extreme climate events. You can now use the Gemini app on Android devices with low memory across the country. Our new Mexico City office will house over one thousand staff members developing global software products. We provided 1.65 million dollars to UNICEF for digital literacy and online safety programs for children. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Sebastian Valverde, Country Managing Director for Google Mexico, explains how our tools are helping local businesses grow and communities stay safe. We are providing precise weather alerts to help people prepare for storms, and we launched a new version of the Gemini app for simpler phones. These updates help students, business owners, and families across Mexico access helpful technology, learn new skills, and stay safe online. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Nearly a year ago, I arrived in Mexico after leading our operations in Miami, with a very clear mission: to continue making Google the best partner for every entrepreneur, business, institution, and person looking to grow here. I knew I was joining a vibrant ecosystem, but reality far exceeded every expectation. In this time, I’ve discovered a country that refuses to be a bystander to the future; Mexico challenges it, embraces it with remarkable speed, and, above all, builds it with its own hands. Going from promise to everyday action For years, we spoke about artificial intelligence as a scientific marvel or an assistant capable of answering questions. Today, however, we are witnessing a fundamental turning point: AI has evolved from providing answers to taking concrete action. It’s no longer just about drafting an email or summarizing a document; it’s about intelligent agents solving complex, multi-step tasks, freeing up valuable time for what truly matters. And when innovation lands in the real world, results are measured in tangible growth. In our latest Economic Impact Report, we confirmed that Google’s tools contributed over 382 billion Mexican pesos in economic activity across Mexico in 2025. Put into perspective, that’s more than 1 billion pesos flowing through local businesses every single day. Behind that number are the real stories that inspire us: for every peso a business invests in Google Ads, it earns an average of eight pesos in commercial return. Whether it’s the neighborhood fonda managing reservations seamlessly or a company modernizing its operations in the cloud, technology only carries real value when it creates shared prosperity. Solving the challenges that matter together At Google for Mexico 2026, we reaffirmed that this potential goes far beyond business. For example, it can help us tackle urgent challenges like climate change and hurricane seasons. Google’s cutting-edge science can provide weather prediction hour by hour, and with up to 15 days in advance. We put that technology to work, partnering closely with the National Water Commission ( CONAGUA ) and the National Meteorological Service to support the forecast for extreme weather events and deliver more precise real-time alerts directly to people’s phones. At the same time, access must never be a luxury. That’s why we are launching the Gemini app for lower memory Android devices in Mexico, redesigned to run smoothly on phones with as little as 2 GB of RAM. Millions of students and local business owners now have access to guided tutoring, voice interaction, and creative assistance in the palm of their hands. And because the future belongs to the next generation, Google.org contributed with $1.65 million in funding to UNICEF to support digital literacy and online safety programmes for children and adolescents across Latin America. In Mexico, UNICEF will use this support to reach more than 300,000 parents, caregivers, teachers and students with practical tools to help prevent and identify online risks early. Building from Mexico for the world Coming soon, we will open our new offices in Mexico City, bringing more than a thousand Googlers together under one roof. Among them are world-class Mexican software engineers already developing global products like Google Chrome. Mexico no longer just uses technology; it creates it, transforms it, and projects it to the world. Being part of this journey is an immense privilege. Let’s keep building a future where technology is, above all, a bridge so that no one is left behind. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. Discover new Genie 3 capabilities While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys. 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images. Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore. Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. Create new interactive experiences The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood. You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds. Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert. Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix. Explore the new gallery When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.” Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring. “Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery. “The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective. The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism. Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix. Learn how we are building responsibly We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview . title: Introducing Stitch Loop: A new way to build and evolve products
body: Introducing Stitch Loop: A new way to build and evolve products Nov 18, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link As part of a new direction for Stitch, we’re introducing a new experiment, Stitch Loop: a long-running product agent that connects to your codebase and live metrics to continuously improve what you’ve shipped. Justin Toupin Director, Product Management, Google Labs Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We are introducing Stitch Loop, a product agent that connects to your codebase and live metrics to continuously optimize your software. It identifies issues, suggests fixes, and opens pull requests to help your team maintain product quality around the clock. You can join the waitlist today at stitch.google.com/loop/waitlist to get started with these automated tools for security, latency, and accessibility. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Justin Toupin introduces Stitch Loop, a product agent that monitors your codebase and metrics continuously. This tool identifies areas for improvement, writes code in a sandbox, and submits pull requests. You maintain full control over all changes because you must approve every pull request manually. The system includes dedicated loops for cybersecurity, latency, and accessibility to help your lean team. You can join the global waitlist today to receive priority access for your development projects. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are introducing Stitch Loop, a new tool from Google Labs that helps you maintain and improve your software after it launches. It connects to your code and live data to find bugs, fix security issues, and boost performance around the clock. You simply review the suggested changes before they go live. This helps your team focus on building new features while the agent handles the ongoing work of keeping your product running well. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Coding agents let you build and ship new features fast, but their job ends the moment your pull request merges. Once code hits production, the real work starts: patching vulnerabilities, speeding up checkout, and diagnosing signup drop-offs buried in noisy feedback. For lean teams, balancing post-launch maintenance with continuous improvement is a constant challenge, yet it’s also what drives some of the world’s most successful products. Today, we are introducing Stitch Loop, a long-running product agent from Google Labs that connects to your codebase and live metrics, finds what needs fixing, and keeps working 24/7 on your product until your goals are met. Millions of designers, developers, and founders already use Stitch to turn ideas into working interfaces in minutes. Together, Stitch and Stitch Loop are steps toward our broader ambition for Stitch: creating agents to help lean teams tackle the hardest parts of creating great products from ideation through continuous optimization. See how it works You start by connecting GitHub and your product context (logs, user behavior, feedback, etc) with over 180 integrations, custom MCP servers, or local CLI uploads. Grounded in that context, Stitch Loop runs evergreen loops to continuously optimize toward the measurable outcomes you care about. You get three default loops out of the box and can add your own anytime. Each loop runs through four steps: Suggestions: Stitch Loop surfaces opportunities to make progress towards your goals, grounded in evidence from your product. Solutions: Every suggestion comes with one or more solutions— each with tradeoffs and scoping, along with visual design options where applicable. Build: Once you choose a direction, Stitch Loop writes the code in an isolated cloud sandbox and opens a GitHub pull request for your approval. When relevant, the PR will contain screenshots and videos of the work Loop did. Reflect: Stitch Loop monitors live product data as it works toward your goal, learning from every positive or negative result to sharpen the next round of insights. Once the goal is met, it keeps watching in case the metric slips. You always have the final call. Nothing merges until you review the PR. Automate codebase security Stitch Loop comes with built-in loops for cybersecurity, latency, and accessibility, plus the ability to create custom loops like improving checkout conversion. Security is often the hardest gap to cover for lean teams shipping quickly. Stitch Loop includes a dedicated security loop that pairs Gemini 4 Carbon's cyber security capabilities with CodeMender , Google DeepMind's autonomous agent that improves code security. Together, they scan your codebase for security vulnerabilities before they become incidents. Stitch Loop flags each issue it finds with evidence and opens a PR with a proposed fix for your review. Use it with your agents and existing workflows You can use Stitch Loop as a service layer for coding agents, like Google Antigravity, or bring it into the places where your team already works, like Slack. Whatever coding agent you prefer can pull persistent product context from Stitch Loop via the Stitch CLI and MCP to power mixed-model setups and fully autonomous improvements in your existing workflow. In Slack, just use @stitch to get daily insight digests and create new loops. Join the waitlist The Stitch Loop waitlist opens today for all users, globally, with eligible Google AI Ultra users getting priority access. Join at stitch.google.com/loop/waitlist and share your feedback in the Google Labs Discord . Get the latest news from Google in your inbox Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription. You can also subscribe with a different email address . Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. title: The Gemini app is now available on lower-memory Android devices.
body: The Gemini app is now available on lower-memory Android devices. Angus Logan Builder, Gemini App Nov 18, 2026 For hundreds of millions of people globally, a lower-memory Android device is their everyday connection to the internet, education, and business. Until recently, hardware limits meant those phones only had basic voice commands. Now, we’re bringing the Gemini app to eligible Android (Go edition) devices , putting Google’s personal AI assistant in the hands of hundreds of millions more people. We re-architected the app so the core Gemini experience runs smoothly on hardware with less memory. Instead of typing out long prompts, you can talk things through or practice for an interview out loud in more than 45 languages with Gemini Live , point your camera at notes or forms to learn and translate, or create custom images with Nano Banana — like a flyer for a weekend bakery sale. To get started, download the Gemini app on Google Play, press and hold the power button on supported phones, or look for it preloaded on upcoming devices from partners like Transsion.
retained_feed_body: The Google Gemini app now supports lower-memory Android devices. Access Gemini Live and custom image creation on your phone. Download the app today.

title: Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025
body: News Release Explore Product View News Release Related Materials Contacts EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 10:00 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 18, 2026 BEA 26–48 Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025 New Statistics for 2025; Updates for 2021–2024 Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1). Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9). Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama ( BEA interactive tables ). Outdoor recreation by activity Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024. Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2): Boating/fishing was the largest conventional activity for the nation at $39.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 35 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($4.5 billion), California ($3.3 billion), and Texas ($3.0 billion). RVing was the second-largest conventional activity for the nation at $26.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 10 states. The states with the largest contributions were Indiana ($4.7 billion), Texas ($2.6 billion), and California ($2.1 billion). Hunting/shooting/trapping was the third-largest conventional activity for the nation at $15.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Arizona and Wyoming. The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($1.8 billion), California ($849.8 million), and Florida ($831.3 million). Snow activities for the nation totaled $7.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Colorado, Utah, and Vermont. The states with the largest contributions were Colorado ($1.8 billion), California ($735.7 million), and Utah ($640.1 million). Outdoor recreation by industry The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation. For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3). Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion). Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion). Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data. Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive . title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
body: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now Systems from ASUS, Dell and MSI are now available — with more from Acer, GIGABYTE, HP and Microsoft on the way — bringing RTX acceleration and up to 128GB of unified memory to local AI, development and creative workflows. November 18, 2026 by Justin Walker 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. A Windows PC Built for Local AI As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops like the ASUS ProArt GR1X mini PC are built to run personal AI agents 24/7. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ Series RTX Spark compact desktop. New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . From Local Agents to AI Creation Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark. Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark. Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting. GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables. Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark. Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work. The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time. DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software. Windows Server 2028 Coming to DGX Station for Windows Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data. Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip is expanding to include support for Windows Server 2028. New accelerator platforms and the breadth of the Windows silicon ecosystem provide customers options at different capability levels and price points for advanced AI development, local inference, and agent workloads at scale. Windows ML Updates Give Developers More Options Also announced at Microsoft Ignite, developers can now bring any GGUF model from Hugging Face and run it within Windows ML using the llama.cpp backend. The DxCGC backend, now available as an experimental release, is an integration for game developers that compiles and runs machine learning models through DirectX 12, allowing them to execute AI workloads alongside graphics. Windows APIs let applications integrate platform-provided AI capabilities adding GPU support for AION Instruct and VSR. Developers can also build high-performance AI models for Windows ML using the command line interface. #ICYMI: The Latest NVIDIA Local AI Updates 🦙 llama.cpp v1.0.0 marks a major milestone for building local AI apps. The open source inference engine introduces API versioning updates, alongside expanded model support and CUDA optimizations for NVFP4 inference. Learn more . 🎉 Ricursive Intelligence introduced its first open model: Ripple-65B Preview. The full-stack AI lab builds self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software and models. Ripple-65B Preview was trained on NVIDIA B300 GPUs, refined using NVIDIA Nemotron post-training datasets and runs locally on DGX Spark. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face . 🤖 Runway’s Praxis-1 is a newly released 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and actions together.
